at.step: A flow network is a directed graph with a source and a sink and a capacity on every edge. At every other vertex, whatever flows in must flow back out. The chapter's own six-vertex graph, now read as six pipes running from a source to a sink.

The dispatcher's own four routes, taken in order: two units down the first, one unit down the second, one unit down the third, three units down the fourth. Seven units shipped in total, and every remaining route now has at least one pipe already full.

Every pipe that already carries flow keeps a second, undo-shaped number beside its forward one: how much of that flow could still be pulled back. Drawn beneath the stuck network, three of its pipes each hide a backward number greater than nothing at all.

A path through this undo-aware graph crosses one pipe backward, pulling back exactly what was sent through it, then keeps going forward the rest of the way to the sink. Pushing as much as that path allows reaches the true maximum: nine units, two more than the stuck count.

Stated as a loop: find any route through the undo-aware graph with room left in either direction, push as much as that route allows, and repeat until no such route remains. A different order of five routes reaches the identical maximum directly, its own last route crossing that identical pipe backward.

When no route remains, the depots still reachable from the source form one side of a split. Every pipe crossing out of that side is completely full; every pipe crossing back carries nothing at all. The flow's own total exactly equals that split's own capacity.

The value of a maximum flow always equals the capacity of a minimum cut. Checked on the chapter's own network, where both numbers lock onto nine, and independently on a second, differently sourced network, where both numbers lock onto twenty-three instead.

If every capacity is a whole number, every route's own push is a whole number too, so the algorithm always ends with a flow that is whole-number everywhere. The consequence used next: give every pipe a capacity of one, and the resulting flow turns out to be either nothing or one on every single pipe.

For whole-number capacities the running time is proportional to the pipe count times the flow's own final value, a bound that can be exponential in the size of the input. One particular four-depot network forces an arbitrary choice of route to take two million one-unit pushes, where a breadth-first choice of route finishes in two. Capacities that are fractions still finish; capacities that are irrational, named only, can loop forever without ever reaching the true maximum.

items.item: A forward-only, no-undo view of a flow network is not merely a worse implementation of the correct algorithm; it is a fundamentally different search that can terminate at a value strictly below the true maximum, because it never considers the one move (crossing a pipe backward) that a correct residual-graph search always has available.

items.item: That the algorithm's own stopping condition (no augmenting path left) and the cut it reads off at that point are the same fact, not two separate things that happen to agree, is the entire content of the constructive half of the max-flow min-cut theorem; the cut is not searched for afterward, it falls out of the reachability computation the algorithm already needed to run to decide whether to stop.

items.item: Integrality is not a property of the final flow discovered by accident; it is an invariant preserved by every single step of the algorithm (each augmentation's own bottleneck is provably a whole number whenever every residual capacity already is), which is why induction on the number of augmentations, not inspection of the final answer, is the right way to prove it.

items.item: A maximum flow's own value being achievable without any flow-carrying cycle is not obvious from the definition of a flow (which permits cycles freely) but follows from a cancellation argument: removing a cycle's own flow changes no vertex's own conservation balance and strictly cannot increase the network's maximum achievable value, so no cycle is ever load-bearing for optimality.

items.item: This chapter's own reduction of a pairing problem to a unit-capacity flow problem (named in the handoff, built in the next topic) depends specifically on integrality, not merely on the max-flow min-cut theorem alone; without integrality, a maximum flow of value k on a unit-capacity network would not by itself guarantee a matching of k edges, since a fractional flow spread thinly across many edges could achieve the same value.

at.step: Ford-Fulkerson ends with a flow and a cut that prove each other optimal, and integrality guarantees that with whole-number capacities the flow is made of whole units. That is exactly what a pairing problem needs. Give every edge capacity one, put a source in front of one side and a sink behind the other, and a maximum flow is a largest set of pairs. How fast can that be done, and what does the cut look like when the capacities are all one? Bipartite matching and Hopcroft–Karp, next.
